facts.fact: Name for the term: "Nitrate"
Name for the term: "NO3-"
Name for the term: "Nitrat"
Name for the term: "NO3"
Nitrate is a byproduct of the nitrogen cycle: bacteria turn ammonia from fish waste into nitrite and then into nitrate.
Nitrate builds up in aquarium water over time.
Nitrate is less toxic than ammonia because fish take it up less readily through their gills.
Nitrate's presence in an aquarium cannot be avoided.
Nitrobacter bacteria convert nitrite (NO2) into nitrate (NO3).
Plants use nitrate as food, so nitrate is needed in planted tanks.
Denitrifying bacteria are anaerobic. They live in substrate or sediment deeper than about 5 cm and turn nitrate into nitrogen gas.
Nitrate shows no visible signs in the water, so it has to be measured with a test kit.
Signs of nitrate poisoning include lethargy, decreased appetite, skin irritation or redness, faster breathing and sudden death.
Nitrate poisoning develops slowly and often goes unnoticed until symptoms appear.
Nitrate poisoning can look like gill parasites or like problems with ammonia, nitrite, pH or temperature.
Vets use a liquid test kit. PetMD says test strips are not reliable for diagnosing water-quality problems.
In an established tank, algae growth is a sign of high nitrate. In a new tank, algae can appear even below 10 ppm.
Many fish show no symptoms at 100 ppm or more, but long exposure makes them more prone to fungal disease and slows growth and reproduction.
At extreme levels, fish become lethargic and develop ulcers or sores on the body.
Fish newly added to a high-nitrate tank can suffer "nitrate shock" and die suddenly, while fish already used to the level usually survive.
Too little nitrate makes plant leaves turn yellow or translucent, starting at the tips, and the leaves eventually melt.
High nitrate can cause algal blooms, which may lower oxygen overnight and cause pH swings.
Most fish tolerate up to 20 mg/L of nitrate. Some species show symptoms at lower levels.
Freshwater fish are generally more tolerant of nitrate than saltwater fish, though sensitivity varies by species.
Therium recommends keeping nitrate at 5–10 ppm and calls 20–50 ppm too high.
Thuysinh4u says nitrate is harmless at low levels but becomes toxic above 20 ppm (20 mg/L).
Aquarium Co-Op recommends keeping fish tanks under 80–100 ppm nitrate, and lower for nitrate-sensitive species.
Aquarium Co-Op says planted tanks should aim for about 50 ppm nitrate, and that 0–20 ppm can cause plant problems.
Aquarium Science reports no evident effect on fish below about 80 ppm, but says shrimp and axolotls may be affected at about 40 ppm.
Aquarium Science says mixed fish and plant tanks commonly run 40–80 ppm, and suggests aiming for orange-red rather than red-red on the API test.
Lab studies report nitrate as nitrogen only (NO3-N). Multiply by about 4.4 to compare with hobby test kits that read NO3. For example, API orange is 40 ppm NO3, while Hach orange is 8 ppm NO3-N.
For juvenile zebrafish (Danio rerio), a study cited by Aquarium Science recommends a limit of 100 mg/L nitrate-nitrogen (about 440 ppm as NO3).
For rainbow trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss), a study cited by Aquarium Science found effects at 80–100 mg/L nitrate-nitrogen (about 352–440 ppm as NO3).
Aquarium Science puts the chronic toxic limit for freshwater fish at about 440–1,200 ppm nitrate, depending on species.
Bacteria and phosphate rise along with nitrate, and algae blooms can lower oxygen.
Causes of high nitrate include waste buildup, infrequent water changes, decaying plant material that is not removed, and overfeeding.
Therium names overfeeding as the main cause of high nitrate.
Too many fish (overstocking) raises nitrate.
Dirty filters raise nitrate, because filter media traps waste without removing it from the system.
Old plant leaves and dead animals or insects left in the tank raise nitrate.
Tap water used for water changes may already contain nitrate, depending on the source.
All-in-one plant fertilizers such as Easy Green raise nitrate because they contain nitrogen.
PetMD's treatment is a partial water change of up to 50%, with the new water dechlorinated and matched to the tank's pH and temperature.
A gravel siphon helps remove debris during the water change.
If low KH (old tank syndrome) has caused low pH, use smaller water changes for a while.
When nitrate is very high, change a small amount of water each day so the fish are not shocked. Once it is down to 5–10 ppm, set up a regular routine.
Aquarium Co-Op suggests a 30–50% water change with a siphon. For very high levels, spread the changes over several days.
Full recovery from nitrate poisoning may take several days to a week.
A 50% water change cuts nitrate by about 50%.
Live plants absorb nitrate. Fast growers such as Pogostemon stellatus work faster than slow growers such as anubias.
Long term, lower nitrate by keeping fewer fish, feeding less or moving to a bigger tank.
In saltwater tanks, well-cured live rock hosts denitrifying bacteria that turn nitrate into nitrogen gas. Daily bacteria doses or a nitrate reactor are also options.
Easy Green dose: 1 pump per 10 gallons, weekly in low light and twice weekly in medium light.
With Easy Green: if nitrate is 50 ppm or more, do 50% water changes until it is 25 ppm or less, then dose up to about 50 ppm.
With Easy Green: if nitrate reaches 75–100 ppm after 3–4 days, change water again and consider removing fish or adding fast-growing plants.
During cycling of a freshwater tank, nitrate starts rising around day 27, when a water change of about 40% is needed.
Test nitrate monthly, and weekly when you add fish, plants or invertebrates, change diet or change filtration.
Replace the liquid test kit yearly, store it indoors and keep a record of the results.
Test your water source, and switch to bottled spring water or reverse-osmosis water if needed.
Feed only what the fish eat in about 2 minutes, split into 2–3 small feedings, and remove leftover food, leaves, dead fish and insects every day.
Estimate how many fish the tank could hold and keep only half that number.
Change water weekly, and clean or replace filter pads, cleaning one filter chamber at a time each week.
Thuysinh4u recommends changing about 30% of the water weekly in freshwater tanks.
Use dechlorinated water for water changes and trim dead plant leaves.
One mistake is skipping fertilizer to keep nitrate down, which starves plants of other nutrients.
Very large water changes can shock fish.
It is a mistake to think any nitrate above 0 ppm is a problem, or to push nitrate as low as possible, which harms plants.
Overfeeding protein raises nitrate.
Aquarium Co-Op says the belief that nitrate is always bad is wrong, because plants need it.
Aquarium Co-Op says fish waste alone is not enough plant fertilizer, because it lacks the right nutrients in the right ratios.
Aquarium Co-Op says fish, snails and shrimp are not harmed by low nitrate. Only plants are.
Aquarium Science says the common advice that nitrate above 10 or 20 ppm harms fish is not supported by the scientific literature.
Aquarium Science disputes that nitrate makes algae thrive, saying high nitrate with fast plant growth helps control algae.
Aquarium Science disputes that any level above 100 ppm is toxic to aquarium fish.
Aquarium Science says tap water above 40 ppm nitrate is usually no reason to panic for adult fish.
Cá Dĩa Đại Phát claims a biological filter turns nitrate into less harmful substances, but nitrate is itself the end product of the cycle in the filter.
